summary: Digestion for ages 11–13: trace food from mouth to large intestine, name each organ and its role (including the liver making bile and the pancreas making enzymes), separate physical from chemical digestion, and explain enzymes simply as biological catalysts that cut large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. The central insight is that digestion is a time-ordered PROCESS converting food you cannot absorb into molecules you can — big into small. Includes a driveable 'follow the food' model, a labelled tract for naming organs, an enzyme-tasting investigation, and optional anatomy/question-answering extensions, with scaffold limits flagged.
misconceptions: Thinking the stomach does most digestion and absorption (the small intestine does most).
Believing food is 'inside the body' once swallowed, rather than passing through a tube until absorbed.
Confusing physical and chemical digestion, or thinking chewing alone is 'digestion'.
Thinking enzymes are alive, or are 'used up' in one reaction (they are catalysts, reused).
Assuming big molecules can be absorbed directly without being broken down.

activities.title: Follow your food: pilot a meal through the gut
steps: Drive a mouthful of food step by step along the tract: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.
At the mouth, trigger both actions: teeth chew (physical) AND saliva's starch enzyme (amylase) begins cutting starch (chemical).
In the stomach, trigger churning plus acid, and a protein-cutting enzyme (protease) starting to break down protein.

In the small intestine, release bile — made by the liver (stored in the gallbladder) — to break a fat blob into small droplets (physical, increasing surface area), then let enzymes from the pancreas and small intestine finish cutting molecules small.
Watch the now-tiny molecules cross the villi into the blood; see water reclaimed in the large intestine.
Try to push a big (undigested) food molecule straight through the gut wall — observe it will not pass until an enzyme has snipped it into small soluble pieces.
Point out where each key enzyme is made (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas/small intestine) and where it acts.
activities.insight: Digestion is an ordered process that physically and chemically breaks food down; big insoluble molecules cannot be absorbed until enzymes cut them into small soluble ones. Physical breakdown (and bile) increases surface area so enzymes work faster.

activities.title: Name the tract: tappable labelled digestive system
steps: Tap each organ along the tract and read its job: mouth (chewing + salivary amylase), oesophagus (carries food down), stomach → 'muscular bag; acid + protease begin protein digestion', liver → 'makes bile that emulsifies fat', pancreas → 'makes digestive enzymes', small intestine → 'enzymes finish digestion; small soluble molecules absorbed here', large intestine → 'reabsorbs water'.
Match each organ to its function and each key enzyme to where it is produced (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas/small intestine).
Use a lift-the-flap check: 'Does the stomach do most absorption?' → reveal 'No — the small intestine does.'
activities.insight: Each organ has a named role in sequence, including the liver (bile) and pancreas (enzymes); absorption happens mainly in the small intestine, not the stomach.

activities.title: The cracker that turns sweet: tasting enzyme action (predict–observe–explain)
steps: Before chewing anything, PREDICT how the taste of a plain cream cracker will change if you chew it slowly and hold it in your mouth for a minute or two, and say why.
After allergy/food-safety checks, chew a plain cream cracker slowly and hold it in the mouth for a minute or two, paying attention to any change in taste.

Observe and record what you actually taste: many people notice a slight sweetness developing as salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars such as maltose, though how strong the effect is varies from person to person.
Explain what happened, distinguishing what teeth do (break into pieces) from what the enzyme does (cut molecules).

Discuss the probe questions: Why can't a tiny bread crumb pass straight into the blood as it is? What is the difference between what your teeth do and what an enzyme does? If enzymes aren't alive, how do they break food down? Where along the gut does most digested food cross into the blood, and why there?
activities.insight: Chemical digestion by an enzyme is a real, directly experienced event — not just breaking food into smaller pieces. Enzymes are catalysts, not living creatures.

activities.title: Sequence and sort: order, categorise, match
steps: Order the organs food passes through from mouth to large intestine.
Categorise examples as physical digestion (chewing, churning, bile emulsifying fat) or chemical digestion (enzymes cutting molecules).
Match each key enzyme to where it is produced and where it acts, and match bile to the liver.
activities.insight: Secure recall and classification: the correct order of organs, the physical/chemical distinction, and enzyme/bile sites.

activities.title: Optional enrichment: fly through the gut and field questions
steps: Take an optional 3D tour along the gut and zoom into a villus to appreciate the folded, large surface area that aids absorption.
Use an optional 'ask an expert' conversation to explore curiosity questions such as 'what happens when you are sick?'
activities.insight: Surface-area anatomy (villi) explains why the small intestine absorbs efficiently; curiosity questions extend engagement without replacing the core process work.

checkQuestion: When you chew bread it breaks into tiny pieces, and your stomach churns it smaller still. A student says 'that's digestion done — the food is now small enough to pass into the blood.' Is breaking food into small pieces enough? If not, what else has to happen to it before it can be absorbed?
checkAnswer: Breaking food into small pieces (physical digestion) is not enough. The large molecules must be chemically broken down by enzymes into small, soluble molecules — starch into glucose, proteins into amino acids, fats into fatty acids — which can then be absorbed through the gut wall into the blood. Physical digestion just increases the surface area for enzymes to work on.
